rendering.title: ATP use in active transport
rendering.body:
Cells spend ATP energy to move ions against their concentration gradients through membrane proteins called ion pumps.

The best-known example is the sodium-potassium ATPase (Na+/K+ pump), found in nearly every animal cell. Here is how it works:

1. The pump protein binds three sodium ions (Na+) from inside the cell and one ATP molecule.
2. ATP is hydrolysed to ADP, releasing energy. This energy changes the shape of the pump protein.
3. The shape change exposes the sodium ions to the outside of the cell, where they are released.
4. Two potassium ions (K+) from outside the cell bind to the pump.
5. The pump returns to its original shape, releasing the potassium ions inside the cell.

The net result: three Na+ are pushed out and two K+ are pulled in per ATP used, both moving against their concentration gradients. This is called active transport because it requires energy input.

Why does this matter? Maintaining these ion gradients is essential for nerve signalling, muscle contraction, and controlling cell volume. Cells devote a large fraction of their ATP budget to running these pumps — in neurons, the Na+/K+ pump can use up to 70% of the cell's ATP.
rendering.summary: Membrane pumps like the sodium-potassium ATPase hydrolyse ATP to move ions against their concentration gradient.
rendering.hint: The sodium-potassium pump moves 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per ATP — can you work out which direction each ion is moving relative to its concentration gradient?
